newsitem.title: USA: Australia has highest gold production costs - Gold Fields.
newsitem.headline: Australia has highest gold production costs - Gold Fields.

text.p: Canada now has the lowest average cost of gold production, while Australia has the highest costs, according to Gold Fields Mineral Services Ltd's (GFMS) 1997 survey of the world gold industry.

"Canada replaced the U.S. as the lowest cost major producer, while Australian costs were the highest in the industry, due in part to currency fluctuations in both Australia and South Africa," one of the report's authors, Philip Klapwijk told New York industry analysts.
World gold production costs rose for the third consecutive year in 1996, although by a smaller margin than in 1995, the report said.
Average cash costs of gold mine production in 1996 were $262 an ounce for the industry worldwide, and average total costs were $317, representing a 1.6 percent and 0.6 percent increase respectively.
Canada, with average cash costs of $222 an ounce and total costs of $282 an ounce, replaced the U.S., with cash costs of $237 an ounce and total costs of $300 an ounce, as the lowest cost producer.
Australia cash costs rose to $294 an ounce, while total costs rose to $358 an ounce, edging out South Africa, with cash costs of $293 and total costs of $334, as the highest cost producer.
The improvement in Canadian costs were made possible by higher grades and better throughput at a large number of established operations where facilities have been expanded, the report said.
In the U.S., the two biggest producers - Barrick and Newmont - which account for 40 percent of output, saw costs rise about seven percent in 1996.

While severe snowfalls in the early months of 1996 impacted on U.S. producer costs, rise in costs are increasingly due to a shift from mining near-surface oxide ores to deeper sulphide ores, the report said.
"Perhaps the most dramatic development in 1996 was the 13 percent increase in Australian cash costs in the same year that (Australia's) gold output reached its highest level ever," the report said.
The increase Australian gold mining costs was due in part to the strengthening of the local currency against the U.S. dollar, the report said.
But operational factors, such as declining grades from deeper open pits led to lower production despite higher throughput, thus increasing costs per ounce of gold produced.
Suppliers of services to the Australian gold mining industry also could not keep up with the higher levels of production, and the resulting delivery delays pushed up costs.
"Under these circumstances, many mines were protected from forced closure only by their aggressive previous hedging of significant proportions of production," the report said.

Production costs in Australia are expected to remain under pressure in the coming year, due to the phasing out of the diesel fuel rebate, and the probable introduction of a state royalty on gold production in Western Australia, which could add $10 an ounce to total cash costs, the report said.
